feedback: If a learner writes 50 cm > 1 m because '50 is bigger', have them line both up on one shared ruler or convert to the same unit (1 m = 100 cm) so the metre visibly towers over the 50 cm; then re-record the true statement 1 m > 50 cm.
If the symbol is reversed (e.g. 32 > 45), re-anchor 'the open side faces the bigger amount' and have them read the statement aloud to check it matches what they mean.
When correct, confirm by reading the full statement aloud with the unit included, e.g. '45 centimetres is greater than 32 centimetres'.
activities.intendedInsight: A measurement is a number together with its unit; you must compare the actual amounts, not the bare digits. When units differ, convert to a shared unit first: 1 m equals 100 cm, which is more than 50 cm, so 1 m > 50 cm even though 1 is a smaller number than 50.
learnerActions: Measure two objects in the same unit and write each measurement with its unit (e.g. a pencil case at 32 cm and a book at 45 cm).
Place >, <, or = between the two readings so the statement is true, then read it aloud ('45 centimetres is greater than 32 centimetres').
Check the symbol points its open side toward the larger amount.

Repeat with a mixed-unit pair, such as a 1 m ribbon and a 50 cm ribbon: before deciding, bring both to the same unit or line them up on one common ruler/scale, then record the true comparison (1 m > 50 cm).
activities.title: Measure, then place the symbol

feedback: If a learner orders by how things look, require the measured value to be written beside each object first, then re-order using only those numbers; discuss the case where looks and measures disagree.
If = is used for measures that are only close, ask them to compare the exact readings and decide whether they are truly equal or whether > or < is correct.
When units differ across the three items, prompt converting to a shared unit or placing them on one common scale before ordering.
activities.intendedInsight: Ordering is done on the measured amounts, not on appearance, and = is reserved for truly equal measures.
learnerActions: Measure three objects (e.g. three containers for capacity) and write the measured value, with its unit, next to each.
Arrange them from least to most by repeatedly picking the smallest remaining measured amount (or from most to least by repeatedly picking the largest remaining measured amount).
Include a case where how big the objects look disagrees with what they measure, and order by the measurements anyway.
Use = only between two measures that are genuinely equal, not merely close.
activities.title: Order three measured things

feedback: Prompt the learner to read each statement aloud with units, confirming the words match the symbol.
Follow a reference check with an actual measure-and-compare task, since reading a fixed example does not by itself show whether the learner can choose and place the symbol for a new pair.
activities.intendedInsight: Secures the meaning and reading of the >, <, = notation as support for making one's own comparisons.
learnerActions: Study a labelled example such as '45 cm > 32 cm' and say what >, <, and = mean ('greater than', 'less than', 'equal to').
Describe why the open side of the symbol faces the larger amount.
Explain in words why a mixed-unit statement like '1 m > 50 cm' is true even though 1 is smaller than 50 (because 1 m is 100 cm).
activities.title: Reference card for the symbols
